Swiss Q2 GDP came in at +1.5% q/q against 0.2-0.4% expected, a pharma-led shock that removes the growth leg from every franc short - CHF is upgraded from -1 to 0 and EUR/CHF and AUD/CHF come off HIGH. Second, Japan: July PPI held 7.2% with yen import prices +29.1%, and Reuters sources now say the joint intervention plus Bessent pushing for an early move have all but LOCKED a Sept 17-18 BoJ hike to 1.25%. JPY goes to -1 MIXED and every yen cross loses a conviction notch even though spot is still pinned at 159.20-159.30. The dollar leg keeps improving for the bears: July PPI printed 4.7% y/y against 5.0% expected and 5.5% prior, core 4.2% from 4.7%, flat m/m - September hike odds are now 32% from 41% Wednesday and 55% a week ago, with Barkin arguing hold and Hammack still demanding a hike. But the dollar index closed FLAT at 100.00, gold FELL 1.3% to 4,347 on falling yields, silver dropped to 64.27 from 66.20, and WTI lost 2% to 81.27 on the same night two ADNOC tankers were attacked in the strait. meta.regime: The regime is still policy differentials, but two of the eight legs snapped overnight and both of them were on the short side of the book. The first is Switzerland. SECO's preliminary Q2 estimate this morning put GDP growth at +1.5% q/q in real terms against a consensus range of 0.2-0.4%, the strongest print in years, driven by the chemical and pharmaceutical sector. The honest caveat is that Swiss pharma output has been distorted for two quarters by exporters front-running US tariffs, so this is not a clean read on domestic demand - but it is emphatically not the picture of a stagnating economy that made the franc a free short next to a zero policy rate, and it lands on top of a services PMI at 63.9 and ZEW at +10. CHF moves from -1 to 0 and the franc crosses all step down. The second is Japan. July PPI held at 7.2% y/y and the yen-based import price index rose 29.1% y/y after 30.1% in June, and Reuters reported that the record joint MoF/US Treasury operation combined with Treasury Secretary Bessent's stated preference for an early Japanese hike have all but locked in a move to 1.25% at the September 17-18 meeting. That is a month earlier than the October window this book has been trading, and it arrives while spot is still stuck at 159.20-159.30 under the 159.36-159.40 ceiling that has now capped four advances since Aug 10. JPY goes to -1 MIXED: the currency is weak, the policy path is not, and yen shorts now carry both an intervention tail and a policy tail. Meanwhile the dollar's fundamental case kept eroding without the price following. July PPI at 4.7% y/y against 5.0% expected, core at 4.2% from 4.7%, the monthly index flat, and September hike odds down to roughly 32% from 41% on Wednesday and 55% a week ago - yet the dollar index closed unchanged at 100.00, gold fell 1.3% to 4,347 into falling Treasury yields, and silver dropped to 64.27 from 66.20. When four separate assets refuse a dovish print, the information is in the refusal. Underneath it all risk appetite is at records: the S&P 500 printed above 7,816, the DAX above 26,450, the Topix a record high, Kospi +4%.

dailyRead: Two theses broke overnight and both of them were shorts, which is why today is a day to cut conviction rather than add it. Start with Switzerland, because it is the cleanest surprise on the board. SECO's preliminary estimate published this morning put Q2 GDP at +1.5% q/q in real terms, against economists' expectations of 0.2% to 0.4%, with the chemical and pharmaceutical industries named as the main driver. The caveat matters and I am not going to bury it - Swiss pharma exports have been distorted for two quarters by front-running ahead of US tariffs, and the 12.5% ceiling the Trump administration has been holding to on Swiss goods gives exporters every reason to pull shipments forward, so some of this reverses. But the franc short was built on a specific picture: zero policy rate, CPI at 0.4% under the SNB's own 0.7% Q3 forecast, producer and import prices deflating at -2.1% y/y, unemployment drifting up to 3.0%, and an economy with no growth argument to offer. That last leg is gone this morning, and it lands on top of a services PMI at 63.9, business confidence at 104 and ZEW at +10. CHF is upgraded from -1 to 0 MIXED. EUR/CHF and AUD/CHF come off HIGH to MEDIUM, GBP/CHF and CAD/CHF to LOW-MED, and USD/CHF flips from RANGE to a low-conviction SHORT because a franc with a growth story beats a dollar whose hike is being priced out. The second break is Japan, and it is the more important one for the book because it touches five pairs. July PPI held at 7.2% y/y - a miss against the 7.4% forecast, but the composition is what counts: the yen-based import price index rose 29.1% y/y after 30.1% in June, which is the currency's own weakness feeding straight into the domestic price level. Reuters reported that the record joint MoF/US Treasury operation at the end of July, together with Treasury Secretary Bessent's expressed desire for an early Japanese hike, have all but locked in a move to 1.25% at the September 17-18 meeting. This book has been trading October as the live window. It is now September, one day after the FOMC, and that changes the shape of every yen cross. JPY moves from -2 to -1 MIXED. Note carefully what has NOT changed: spot is still 159.20-159.30, the 159.36-159.40 band has now capped four advances since Aug 10, and the yen was one of the currencies the dollar GAINED against on Thursday. The currency is still weak. But a weak currency with a hawkish central bank one month out and an active intervention mandate is not a currency to be short with size, so EUR/JPY, AUD/JPY and GBP/JPY all come down from HIGH to MEDIUM, JPYBASKET goes to RANGE, and USD/JPY becomes a low-conviction SHORT into the 159.40 ceiling rather than a RANGE trade. Now the dollar, where the fundamentals and the price are openly disagreeing. July PPI printed 4.7% y/y against 5.0% expected and 5.5% in June, core PPI 4.2% from 4.7%, and the monthly index was FLAT against a 0.1-0.2% expected rise, with final demand goods falling 0.7% on energy and only services (+0.2%) and construction (+2.2%) pushing back. Money markets cut September hike odds to roughly 32.4% from 40.6% on Wednesday and 55% a week ago. Initial claims came in at 209,000 against 204,000 expected. Fed speakers split cleanly - Barkin argued for holding given cooling inflation, Hammack repeated her call to raise now. That is a materially weaker dollar case than 24 hours ago. And yet: the dollar index closed unchanged at 100.00, having recovered from its lows; the dollar GAINED on the day against the franc, kiwi, yen, pound and Aussie, losing only to the euro and the loonie; gold fell 1.3% to close near 4,347 despite the 10-year dropping to about 4.6%; and silver fell from 66.20 to 64.27. Four assets that should have rallied on a soft PPI did not. I read that as positioning rather than a change in the fundamental direction - the short-dollar trade is crowded going into Jackson Hole on Aug 27 - but it is a reason to hold existing dollar shorts rather than press them, and it is why XAU/USD goes to RANGE and XAG/USD is downgraded to LOW-MED after one session as the highest-conviction metal on the sheet. The euro remains the top score at +2 and is unchanged: HICP 2.9% with core UP to 2.5%, services 3.3%, deposit facility 2.25% verified on TE, Sept 10 still around 70% priced, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y with the second estimate at 09:00Z today. The one caution I will flag is that TE's own ECB commentary now describes the post-July tone as wait-and-see, citing softer inflation, wage growth, activity and inflation expectations - and euro-area consumer inflation expectations did fall to 3.0% from 3.5%. The hike is not at risk yet, but the September 10 meeting is no longer a formality and the euro's +2 rests on it. Australia holds +2 on the August Statement on Monetary Policy - underlying inflation 3.3% by end-2026, no return to the 2-3% midpoint until early 2028, risks skewed UP - even though the Aussie softened on Thursday after Assistant Governor Kent called policy only somewhat restrictive, a reading the market took as more dovish than the substance justified. Governor Bullock spoke overnight at 23:30Z; her August 11 framing that the economy is operating above capacity is the anchor until something contradicts it. Sterling stays +1 after Q2 GDP confirmed +0.4% q/q with the y/y rate accelerating to 1.2% from 0.9%, though the June trade deficit widened sharply to GBP 5.54bn from 1.04bn and RICS house prices are at -30, so the upgrade is not a strong one. Canada stays +1 and was one of only two currencies to gain on the dollar Thursday: the +75,100 July jobs print and 6.4% unemployment are untouched, but crude fell another 2% and the terms-of-trade leg keeps thinning. New Zealand stays at -2 and remains the single cleanest short - Q3 business inflation expectations at 2.34% against a 2.7% forecast and 2.53% prior, with unemployment at 5.6% and the ANZ commodity index decelerating to +0.5% y/y. Finally the oil complex, where the non-confirmation is loud. Two ADNOC vessels were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday evening and the UAE publicly blamed Iran; the IEA warned that reopening the strait is becoming urgent because the world is burning through stockpiles; only 14 vessels transited on Tuesday. And WTI still fell about 2% to settle near 81.50 and trades 81.27 this morning, with Brent at 87.18. A market that will not rally on tanker attacks is a market that has already priced the closure and is now trading the 17.4-million-barrel inventory build and the 1.6mb/d demand destruction the IEA has penciled in for 2026. USOIL stays RANGE. Today's tests are US retail sales at 12:30Z - the consumer check with wage growth at 3.2% now below headline inflation at 3.4% - and the Michigan preliminary inflation expectations at 14:00Z, which is the cleanest read available on whether the energy shock is reaching household expectations the way it failed to reach New Zealand's.

USD.note: Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 for a fifth straight meeting with THREE dissents FOR a hike, and Chair Warsh declined to give guidance or submit a dot. Every input since has cut the same way. Aug 7 payrolls: July nonfarm payrolls CONTRACTED by 23,000 against +83,000 to +95,000 expected, prior two months revised down by a combined 146,000, and the fall in unemployment to 4.1% from 4.2% is a participation artefact with participation at a five-year low of 61.4%; average hourly earnings slowed to 3.2% y/y, the weakest since May 2021. Aug 12 CPI: 3.4% headline from 3.5% and core 2.5% from 2.6%, both exactly at consensus, +0.1% m/m with shelter about two thirds of it, and no visible pass-through from the crude surge. Aug 13 PPI, the decisive one: final demand 4.7% y/y against 5.0% expected and 5.5% in June, core PPI 4.2% from 4.7%, and the monthly index FLAT against 0.1-0.2% expected - final demand goods fell 0.7% on energy while services rose only 0.2% and construction 2.2%. Money markets now price roughly a 32.4% chance of a September hike, down from 40.6% on Wednesday and 55% a week ago; TE carries the policy rate at 3.75% upper bound. Initial claims came in at 209,000 against 204,000 expected, a touch soft. The committee is openly split: Richmond's Barkin argued for holding given cooling inflation while acknowledging embedded-price risk, Cleveland's Hammack questioned whether the slowdown holds and repeated her call to hike now, and Lisa Cook has said she is prepared to raise. Q2 GDP 1.5% annualised, GDP annual 2.1%. What has NOT happened is any price confirmation - the dollar index closed unchanged at 100.00 and gained against five of the seven majors. Retail sales today at 12:30Z and Michigan inflation expectations at 14:00Z are the next inputs, then Jackson Hole on Aug 27, where Warsh has to say whether the deferred energy tail still counts.

EUR.when: Sept 10 (~70% priced, but no longer a formality)
EUR.note: Deposit facility 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike, headline refi 2.40% and marginal lending 2.65%, all confirmed unchanged on Jul 23 and re-verified on TE this morning. TE's model still carries 2.65% on the refi by end-September, i.e. one more 25bp move. The domestic case is the reason EUR holds the top score and it stands entirely on its own: July HICP 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5% and services inflation 3.3%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y with the second estimate at 09:00Z today, final composite PMI 52.0 with services 51.7 and manufacturing 51.9, wage growth 3.4%, unemployment 6.3% and stable, ZEW 23.4 from 9.5, energy inflation accelerating to 10.0% from 8.5%. Lagarde's July framing - that the longer energy prices stay elevated the more likely they drive broader inflation through indirect and second-round effects - survives Brent at 87.18 rather than 92. The new caution, and I am flagging it because it has hardened: TE's own ECB coverage now characterises the post-July stance as an explicit wait-and-see, citing softer inflation, wage growth, economic activity AND inflation expectations as having reduced the urgency for another move, and euro-area consumer inflation expectations did fall to 3.0% from 3.5%. Add pipeline disinflation - producer prices decelerating to 4.6% y/y from 5.9% with the monthly index at -0.3%, food inflation 1.2%, June retail sales -0.3% m/m and industrial production flat. The hike is still the base case and nothing between Jul 23 and today has taken it off the curve, but September 10 is a real meeting now, not a formality, and the euro's +2 is levered to it.

GBP.note: Held 3.75% on Jul 30 but 6-3, a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus, verified on TE today. The two-week data vacuum is now filled and it resolved firm on the parts that matter to the MPC. Tuesday's labour report: unemployment 4.9% with 1.76 million unemployed, wages 4.3% including bonuses and 3.4% excluding, real pay positive at 1.3% and 0.4%, employment change +148,000. Thursday's Q2 GDP: +0.4% q/q against +0.3% expected, a slowdown from Q1's +0.6% but with the y/y rate ACCELERATING to 1.2% from 0.9%, and June monthly GDP at +0.3% against an expected decline. June CPI 2.6% headline and core with services at 3.6%. An economy accelerating on a y/y basis does not fold three dissenters on the most inflation-sensitive committee in the G10, and TE's end-of-quarter forecast is 4.00%. The offsetting detail from the same session is worth respecting: the June trade deficit widened sharply to GBP 5.54bn from 1.04bn against a 3.6bn forecast, industrial production was soft, and the RICS house price balance sits at -30. The labour market's edges also keep fraying - vacancies at 712,000 below pre-pandemic levels, economic inactivity rising to 9.11 million at a 20.9% rate, claimant count +6.7k. Sterling was one of the currencies the dollar gained against on Thursday despite the GDP beat. July CPI around Aug 19 is the input that decides whether the +1 survives.

JPY.when: Sept 18 (Reuters: intervention plus Bessent have all but locked it)
JPY.note: MOVED FORWARD A MONTH. Held 1.00% on Jul 31 8-1, Takata dissenting for 1.25%, and this book has been trading October as the live window. That changed on Aug 12-13. July PPI held at 7.2% y/y - technically a miss against the 7.4% forecast - but the yen-based import price index rose 29.1% y/y after a 30.1% surge in June, which is the currency's own weakness feeding directly into the domestic price level, and Reuters reported that the record joint Japan-US intervention combined with Treasury Secretary Bessent's stated desire for an early Japanese hike have all but locked in a move to 1.25% at the September 17-18 meeting - one day after the FOMC. The domestic case was already the best in three decades: June labour cash earnings +3.4% y/y with base pay accelerating to 3.4%, real earnings positive for a sixth month, nominal growth above 3% for five straight months, the longest run in 34 years; June CPI 1.7% from 1.5% with core 1.6%; Tokyo July core CPI 1.9% from 1.6% and Tokyo CPI ex food and energy at 2.0%. The Bank has warned for the first time that underlying inflation could exceed target. What has not changed is the spot market: the yen is still 159.20-159.30, the 159.36-159.40 band has capped a fourth advance since Aug 10, the trade balance is -JPY 407bn with terms of trade deteriorating to 81.62 from 82.71, and the dollar GAINED against the yen on Thursday. So the currency is weak and the policy path is not, which is exactly why JPY moves from -2 to -1 MIXED rather than staying a clean short. Practically: yen shorts now carry an intervention tail near 160 AND a policy tail into Sept 18. Cut size, keep the crosses over USD/JPY. Q2 GDP lands Aug 16 23:50Z and July national CPI around Aug 20 23:30Z.

AUD.note: Held the cash rate at 4.35% on Aug 11 as all 37 Reuters economists expected, verified on TE today, and the tone did the work: Bullock said the domestic economy is operating ABOVE CAPACITY and that growth will need to slow to bring inflation down, and the statement retained 'including increasing the cash rate target further if required' with no qualification. The August Statement on Monetary Policy is the hawkish anchor and it has not been touched - underlying inflation forecast at 3.3% by end-2026, no return to the middle of the 2-3% band until early 2028, and risks to inflation explicitly skewed to the UPSIDE, citing elevated energy prices and strong AI-related demand. That is the highest policy rate in the G10 after three hikes in 2026. Against it, Assistant Governor Kent said on Thursday that policy is only 'somewhat restrictive', that earlier tightening is working as intended, and named the Australian dollar's own appreciation as part of the restraint. The Aussie sold off on it, and the honest note from the tape is that the market read Kent as more dovish than the substance of his comments arguably supported - he pointedly stopped short of calling policy sufficiently restrictive. Governor Bullock spoke overnight at 23:30Z, the first chance to correct or confirm that read. Q2 detail supports the hawks: headline CPI cooled to 3.8% from 4.0% and trimmed mean rose to 3.6%, but the WEIGHTED MEDIAN ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5% and services inflation to 4.0%. Labour solid at employment +76,343 and unemployment 4.4% with participation 67.0%; July PMIs services 53.6, composite 53.2, manufacturing 52.0; consumer confidence 83.9 and +4.1% m/m; commodity prices +15.4% y/y. TE's model carries 4.60%. The dovish crack remains July consumer inflation expectations at 4.7% from 5.5%.

NZD.when: Sept 2 (the hike is off and the survey settled it)
NZD.note: OCR raised 25bp to 2.50% on Jul 8, the first hike in three years, verified on TE, and that cycle is finished with the evidence to prove it. Wednesday's RBNZ quarterly survey was the confirmation and it missed badly: Q3 two-year business inflation expectations came in at 2.34% against a 2.7% FORECAST and 2.53% prior, the lowest since Q4 2025, with one-year expectations collapsing to 2.60% from 3.41% - one of the largest single-quarter falls in the series. Only the five- and ten-year tails ticked up, to 2.31% and 2.20%. The risk this book had flagged against the kiwi short was a JUMP in expectations forcing a rethink; it went decisively the other way, which says the imported-inflation channel that drove Q2 CPI to 4.1% - 27.5% of it petrol - is not reaching what businesses actually expect, and crude has since fallen another 2% to WTI 81.27, removing more of the fuel. Note the survey's own OCR question still shows respondents expecting 2.73% by end-September, but that section was run on stale footing relative to the May decision and is contradicted by the expectations data itself. The labour side is the worst in the G10: Q2 unemployment 5.6% against 5.4% expected, the highest since Q3 2015, unemployed persons 171,000, underutilisation 13.8%, wage growth just 2.1% y/y, and employment +0.5% q/q only because participation climbed to 70.7% from 70.4%. Core inflation 3.2%. The offset is domestic sentiment - July ANZ business confidence 56.1 from 36.6, ANZ Roy Morgan consumer confidence 99.3, manufacturing PMI 59.7, composite 53.6 - but ANZ commodity prices decelerated to +0.5% y/y from +2.7% and the Global Dairy Trade index rose only 0.1%, so the terms-of-trade support is gone too. Business NZ PMI for July lands tonight at 22:30Z.

CAD.note: Held 2.25% on Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting, re-verified on TE this morning, and the inflation side keeps it there - June CPI 2.8% with CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9%, both BELOW target, core at 2.1% and CPI-common 2.6%. The labour leg is intact and is still the best in the G10: July employment rose 75,100, the largest gain in two years, with full-time +38,600 and part-time +36,600, unemployment falling to a two-year low of 6.4% from 6.5%, participation rising to 65.1%, employment rate 60.9% and youth unemployment down to 12.6%. Wage growth is a soft 3.4% y/y with average hourly earnings at CAD 38.61, which is why this is a growth story and not a rate one. The commodity leg keeps thinning: WTI fell about 2% on Thursday to settle near 81.50 and trades 81.27 this morning with Brent at 87.18, terms of trade have fallen to 101 from 107, commodity prices decelerated to +20.7% y/y from 33.4%, and oil exports dropped to CAD 13.26bn from 14.92bn - all of which is happening even as tankers are being attacked in the strait, which tells you the market has priced the closure. Offsetting that, the loonie was one of only two currencies to GAIN on the dollar on Thursday, the trade surplus widened to CAD 3.86bn, manufacturing PMI is 53.5 and small-business sentiment jumped to 58.3. Q1 GDP flat at 0.0% q/q with GDP annual -0.1% and monthly GDP +0.2% in June. July CPI is due around Aug 18.

CHF.when: Sept 24 (SNB) — but the growth argument just changed
CHF.note: At ZERO since mid-2025, held in Dec, Mar and Jun, verified on TE today; panellists still see no change until 2027 and the SNB's June statement pledged to lean against rapid APPRECIATION only. The inflation picture is unchanged and remains the core of the dovish case: July CPI 0.4% y/y against 0.5% expected and down from 0.5%, core unchanged at 0.3%, both under the SNB's own 0.7% Q3 conditional forecast, and producer and import prices deflating at -2.1% y/y for a second month against a -1.6% forecast. Unemployment has drifted up to 3.0% from 2.9% with 139,276 unemployed. What changed this morning is the growth leg. SECO's preliminary Q2 estimate put real GDP growth at +1.5% q/q against economists' expectations of 0.2% to 0.4%, with the chemical and pharmaceutical industries named as the main driver. Treat the level with care - Swiss pharma output has been distorted for two quarters by exporters front-running US tariffs under the 12.5% ceiling, so part of this reverses in Q3 - but the franc short was built on a currency with zero rate, no inflation AND no growth, and the third leg is now gone. It sits alongside a services PMI at 63.9 from 59.8, business confidence at 104 and ZEW at +10 from -25. CHF is upgraded from -1 to 0 MIXED. This does not make the franc a long: the SNB is pinned at zero for at least another quarter, FX reserves rose to CHF 768.3bn in July from 758.9bn showing the bank is still active, and the franc was one of the currencies the dollar gained against on Thursday. It makes the franc shorts a MEDIUM rather than a HIGH, and it means USD/CHF stops being a pure cancellation trade.

geopolitics: The war escalated on the water and softened in the rhetoric within the same twenty-four hours, and crude ignored both. On the escalation side: two ADNOC vessels were attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday evening, with the UAE strongly condemning what it called a hostile Iranian attack and Iran declining to comment - the second strike on Emirati-affiliated shipping this month after the Aug 8 incident. Traffic remains a fraction of normal, with only 14 vessels crossing on Tuesday even a day after Trump publicly claimed the waterway is open and under Washington's control, and the IEA warned this week that reopening is becoming pressing because the world is drawing down oil stockpiles fast, having already cut its 2026 demand forecast by 1.6 million barrels a day. On the de-escalation side: a senior Iranian official said Friday that now is the best time for an agreement with the US and proposed the earlier Islamabad framework as the basis for talks, which sits alongside Vice President Vance's claim that Iran has told Washington it has no plans to impose tolls. Tehran's formal conditions have not moved - lift the naval blockade, lift sanctions, withdraw US forces, pay reparations, release frozen assets - and it is still negotiating only through Oman. What matters for FX is that the price refused both narratives. WTI fell about 2% on Thursday to settle near 81.50 and trades 81.27 this morning, Brent is 87.18, and this happened on the night the tankers were hit. A market that will not bid on a tanker strike has already discounted the closure and is now trading the 17.4-million-barrel US inventory build and the IEA's demand destruction instead. The FX consequences follow directly. Canada is now a one-leg currency: the labour market carries it, the terms-of-trade channel is dead, and every CAD-versus-oil expression steps down. New Zealand loses the last of the imported-petrol argument at exactly the moment its inflation expectations missed at 2.34%. The euro is barely affected because Lagarde's second-round case rests on Brent near 87 being high, not on Brent going higher. Japan gets marginal relief on a JPY 407bn trade deficit but its terms of trade still fell to 81.62 from 82.71. And the two haven currencies are capped from opposite directions - the franc by a growth surprise that gives it a non-haven reason to be bid, the yen by an official sector that has already intervened once. Equities confirm the risk-on read with the S&P above 7,816, the DAX above 26,450 and the Topix at a record. The asymmetry to respect is unchanged: the June 14-point MoU unravelled within days of signing, so a deal headline is reversible, and the one thing that would put the premium back faster than it came out is a strike on export infrastructure rather than on shipping.
